4858-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
The Spanish Armada reaches Calais roads in August 1588, and John Lothrop Motley narrates the tense pause before its fate is sealed. Medina Sidonia's great fleet anchors on Saturday afternoon, August 6, expecting to join Parma's army, while Lord Henry Seymour's squadron watches from between Dungeness and Folkestone.

No shots are fired at first, and coasting vessels bring no news, leaving both sides waiting on wind, tide, and Parma's embarkation. Motley builds the scene from the fleets' positions and the plans each commander carried. Readers feel the weight of a long-prepared invasion hanging on a single junction that never quite happens as designed.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1588d:
John Lothrop Motley reaches the Armada's climax in the second part of chapter nineteen of his History. The English fleet drops anchor near Calais, within a mile and a half of the Spaniards. Lord Henry Seymour's junction completes the combined force. That invincible armada has at last almost reached its destination.

Parma's veterans wait on shore, disciplined on a hundred battlefields, to embark for England. A night of anxiety precedes the fireships and the running fight up the Channel. Motley writes the scene as the hinge of his whole history. The republic's survival, England's safety, and Spain's decline meet off Calais roads. His sympathy is wholly with the defenders. Readers get the campaign from the Dutch side of the water, where small ships and shallow coasts defeated an empire's design.
uslaw-usc-t2-s168d:
Section 168d of Title 2 of the United States Code authorizes money for the Constitution Annotated. That work is the government's annotated edition of the Constitution, prepared under sections 168 to 168d. It explains the Constitution through the cases decided under it.

The whole section is a single sentence. It authorizes the appropriation of such sums as may be necessary. The sums serve to carry out the provisions of the four sections named. The money is to remain available until expended, with no yearly lapse. The open amount and open term suit a reference work that is revised forever.
uslaw-usc-t2-s288d:
Section 288d of Title 2 of the United States Code arms the Senate Legal Counsel to enforce Senate subpoenas in court. A subpoena ignored is a challenge to the Senate's power to investigate. This section turns defiance into a civil case.

When directed under section 288b(b), the Counsel shall bring a civil action. The suit may be filed in any court of the United States with jurisdiction. One cited route is section 1365 of Title 28, the Senate subpoena statute. The action can seek three ends. It can enforce the subpoena or order outright. It can ask a court to declare the subpoena's validity. Or it can head off a threatened failure or refusal to comply. The subpoenas covered are those of the Senate or of its authorized committees and subcommittees.
uslaw-usc-t2-s28d:
Section 28d of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with sets of the Precedents. The Director of the Government Publishing Office hands the sets out. The sets go to named offices and libraries for official use in their work. Each standing or joint panel of Congress gets four sets of the work.

The House Legislative Counsel office gets five sets under the same rule. The Senate Legislative Counsel office gets five sets by the same count. The House library gets four sets and the Senate library gets two. The Supreme Court library gets nine sets, the largest count in the list. The debate reporters' offices of each house get three sets each. A second part deals with the marks on each set and who owns it.
uslaw-usc-t2-s658d:
Section 658d of Title 2 of the United States Code bars some bills from debate. It sits in the part on federal mandates in budget work. A bill or joint measure may not be taken up in either house in one case. That case is a missing statement from the Budget Office Director.

The statement must give the direct costs of federal mandates in the bill. The panel that reports the bill must print the statement first in time. A second bar hits bills that push mandate costs past set caps. Such a bill is in order only if it gives new funds or rights. The text sets which house each form of new power must sit in. The rest of the section works through the point of order path.
